title: The key to consistency
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino argues that consistent application of behaviour policy, across teachers, classes and the whole school, is the foundation on which student habits and trust are built. Two scenarios, a student receiving one of three deserved comments and two teachers of one class holding different standards, show how inconsistency undermines newer teachers and confuses students. She then diagnoses why consistency is hard: teachers who do not value a rule, unclear messaging, unclear reasoning, entrenched habits, and long-serving staff who have outlived policy changes. Her responses are clear definitions, explained reasoning, habit-replacement scripts and stable policies, with an honest note that she is not a senior leader.
points: Consistency has to exist across lessons, year groups and the whole school; being consistent only in your own room still leaves students with a mixed message.
Inconsistency is usually not laziness; it comes from rules teachers do not value, vague definitions such as low-level disruption, or unexplained rationale.
Habit research suggests replacing a sub-optimal response with a better one at the same environmental cue and rehearsing it, for example through scripts.
Policies that change drastically and often give experienced staff little reason to invest, so stability matters as much as content.
Leaders should reduce controllable drivers of reverting to old habits, such as workload and fear of performance assessment.
quotes: It has been said in many great edubooks that consistency is key. In fact, it is the ‘foundation of all habits’ (Bennett, T. 2020), and is key in ensuring students trust their teacher (Mccrea, P. 2020). We need consistency of the application of policies, rules, and routines in lessons, in classes, in year groups and, indeed, the whole school. Without this, the system breaks down and students get a confused message from their teachers.

Rules need to be absolutely clear to both teachers and students. If school leaders don’t have the same standards, or if different documentation state different levels of acceptance of behaviours, then there can be confusion about applying the rule.
When implementing a policy, all staff and students should be aware of the why as well as the how. Problems arise when students believe a rule is there purely to upset them

It has dawned on me in recent years that most of my problems in the classroom in terms of poor behaviour disappear when everyone (and I mean everyone) in school follows the same rules consistently. For this to happen, it is so important that, whatever the rule, the reasoning is communicated clearly and reiterated regularly.
Hobbiss et al suggest replacing a sub-optimal habit with an effective one when the same environmental cues that trigger the former occur, and then to repeat this a number of times.
